On The Art of Noticing

I want to talk about noticing.

Not the big, obvious kind of noticing — like noticing a fire alarm or a billboard or that someone has changed their hair. I mean the quiet kind. The kind that happens in the corner of your eye and almost doesn't happen at all. Because I think most of life is lived in that almost-space, and we miss it entirely.

Let me explain what I mean.

There is a Japanese concept called *komorebi*. It describes sunlight filtering through leaves, the way it dances on the ground when the wind moves. There is no single English word for that. We have to use a whole sentence to say it, and even then we don't quite capture it. But the thing itself happens every single day, in every park and on every tree-lined street. It's been happening for millions of years before anyone thought to name it. The light was always doing that. We were just not looking.

I think about that a lot. How many phenomena are happening right now that we don't have words for, and therefore don't really see?

For most of human history, people looked up at the night sky and saw a milky smear of light. They called it milk, or a river, or a road of straw. It wasn't until we had telescopes powerful enough and minds curious enough that we realized that smear was actually a hundred billion stars, each perhaps with planets, and that our own sun was just one unremarkable member of that crowd. The sky didn't change. Our noticing changed.

And that makes me wonder what we are looking at right now, every day, that we are completely misinterpreting because we lack the right lens.

Take a simple object. A coffee mug on your desk.

If you are not noticing, it is just a mug. It's ceramic, it holds coffee, it has a chip on the handle. End of story.

If you start noticing, the mug becomes an archive. The clay was dug from the ground somewhere, perhaps in China or Germany, formed by hands or by a machine that was designed by hands. It was fired at over a thousand degrees, glazed, shipped in a container across an ocean on a ship burning fuel made from plankton that died 300 million years ago. Someone designed the logo on it. Someone else chose the exact curve of the handle so it would feel comfortable to a human hand. Every single mug is a culmination of geology, industrial design, global logistics, and human habit. And then *you* chose it. Or someone gave it to you. It has a history in your life too — the morning you bought it at a thrift store, the time you left it on the roof of your car and somehow it didn't fall.

Suddenly the mug is not an object. It's a story with a handle.

This is what happens when you practice noticing. The world goes from flat to deep. From wallpaper to a library.

And the strange thing is, we are biologically wired *not* to do this. Our brains are prediction machines. They are designed to conserve energy. So they create models of the world and then they stop checking. This is called habituation. When you first move into a new apartment, you notice the way the floorboards creak in the hallway, the hum of the refrigerator, the exact color of the light at 5 p.m. A week later, you notice none of it. Your brain has filed it under "known" and moved on. It is efficient, but it makes us blind.

Artists, writers, scientists, and children are just people who have figured out how to fight habituation. Or who never learned it in the first place.

A child will crouch for ten minutes and watch ants carry crumbs. Not because the child has more free time than you, though they do, but because the child's brain has not yet learned to label "ants carrying crumbs" as boring and therefore invisible. To a child, it is still a drama, a logistics operation, a mystery.

We can get that back. We can practice unlabeling the world.

Here's an exercise I love: Pick one ordinary walk that you do often — from your door to the bus stop, from your kitchen to your bedroom — and force yourself to find five things you have never seen before. Not big things. Tiny things. The rust pattern on a fire hydrant. The way a particular vine has wrapped itself around a fence. A single cracked tile that looks like a map of Italy. The sound the crosswalk makes when it's windy.

The first time you do it, it feels forced. The fifth time, it feels like a game. By the twentieth time, your brain has rewired slightly. You start to notice without trying. The walk becomes longer, not in distance but in richness. You arrive at the same bus stop but you have lived more on the way there.

This matters because attention is the substance of our lives. We like to think our lives are made of years and months, but really they are made of moments of attention. If most of those moments are spent on autopilot — scrolling, worrying, half-listening — then our lives feel short and blurry. If we can reclaim even a fraction of our attention for real noticing, time dilates.

Think about vacations. Why does a one-week vacation in a new country feel longer in memory than three months of routine at home? It's not because time actually slowed down. It's because you were noticing more. Your brain was recording more densely. More novelty equals more memory anchors, which equals a longer-feeling life. You don't need a plane ticket to get that effect. You just need to treat your own street like a new country.

There is another side to this, of course. Noticing can be painful. If you start really looking, you will see not just the beautiful komorebi but also the loneliness on the subway, the plastic in the gutter, the exhaustion in a friend's eyes that they are trying to hide. When you open the aperture, all the light comes in, not just the pretty light. This is why habituation is a defense mechanism. It protects us from being overwhelmed.

But the alternative — staying numb — is more expensive. You pay for it with a life that feels thin.

So the trick is not to notice everything all at once forever. It's to choose to notice deeply for short periods. To have moments of intentional, generous attention. What the poet Mary Oliver called “attention is the beginning of devotion.”

She had a practice of walking in the woods every day and paying such close attention that she could write poems about grasshoppers and ponds that made people weep. She wasn't seeing a different forest than anyone else. She was *looking* at the same forest differently.

I think about what would happen if we all did this a little more. If we taught noticing in schools alongside math. If we had five minutes of silence in every workday just to look out a window without an agenda. If we asked people not "What do you do?" but "What have you noticed lately?"

We would be a little slower, probably. A little less productive in the spreadsheet sense. But I think we would be more human. We would be better at empathy, because empathy is just noticing another person's interior life. We would be better at science, because science is just noticing what everyone else ignored. We would be better at love, because love is — more than anything — sustained, fascinated attention to another person long after your brain wants to file them under "known."

Recently I was sitting in a laundromat waiting for my clothes to dry. It's not a place you'd expect to have a profound experience. Fluorescent lights, plastic chairs, the smell of detergent. I was about to pull out my phone, out of habit, when I decided to just look.

I noticed the dryers all had little portholes, and the clothes tumbling inside looked like strange planets in orbit. I noticed that one dryer was squeaking in a rhythm that almost sounded like music. I noticed an old woman folding her husband's shirts with a care that suggested she had been folding his shirts for fifty years and still found meaning in it. I noticed a teenager doing homework, mouthing the words silently, completely absorbed. I noticed my own sock, alone and turned inside out, tumbling bravely by itself.

For ten minutes, a boring errand became a small film. Nothing had changed except my attention.

And that's the secret. The world does not need to become more interesting. We need to become more interested.

There is enough wonder in a single square meter of ground, if you look closely enough, to fill a lifetime. There are cities inside a speck of soil. There are dramas on your windowsill. There are galaxies in the way light falls through your blinds at 4 p.m.

You don't have to go anywhere to find something extraordinary. You just have to stop, for a moment, and truly see where you already are.

So today, wherever you are while reading this — in a kitchen, on a train, in bed — pause for thirty seconds after you finish. Look up. Find one thing you have never truly seen before. Give it your full, quiet attention. Let it be interesting without needing it to be useful.

That's all. That's the whole practice.

The world has been waiting to be noticed by you.
